kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-04.title: Binary
kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-04.body:
In binary, $100 = 1100100_2$, i.e. $100 = 64 + 32 + 4$: three powers of two.

Two powers are not enough: if $2^a + 2^b = 100$ with $a \ge b$, the larger one is at least 50 and less than 100, so it is 64, and then $2^b = 36$, which is not a power of 2. One power is not enough either, since 100 is not a power of 2.

**Answer: (B) 3**

kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-04.title: Greedy
kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-04.body:
Take the largest power of two that fits each time: $100 - 64 = 36$, $36 - 32 = 4$, $4 - 4 = 0$. That uses 3 powers. Using a smaller power than 64 at the start would leave more to cover (e.g. $100 = 32 + 32 + 32 + 4$ needs 4), and a single power or two powers cannot give 100 (64 plus another power never makes 100).

**Answer: (B) 3**

kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-08.title: Equation
kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-08.body:
We need $\frac1x = 4x$, so $4x^2 = 1$, $x^2 = \frac14$ and (being positive) $x = \frac12$.

Check: the reciprocal of $\frac12$ is 2, and $4 \cdot \frac12 = 2$. ✓

**Answer: (B)** $\frac{1}{2}$

kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-08.title: Test the choices
kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-08.body:
- $\frac14$: reciprocal 4, quadruple 1. ✗
- $\frac12$: reciprocal 2, quadruple 2. ✓
- 1: reciprocal 1, quadruple 4. ✗
- 2 and 4 have reciprocals below 1 but quadruples above 1. ✗

**Answer: (B)** $\frac{1}{2}$

kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-15.title: Three pushes work, two don't
kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-15.body:
Push the three lamps of the top row. A lamp in the top row is changed by all three pushes (they are all in its row): 3 changes, so it ends up off. A lamp in another row is changed only by the push in its own column: 1 change, so it is off too. All 9 lamps are off after 3 pushes.

Fewer is impossible. With at most two pushes, the pushed lamps lie in at most two rows and at most two columns. So some lamp lies in a third row and a third column; no push changes it and it stays on.

**Answer: (A) 3**

kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-15.title: Count changes
kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-15.body:
Each lamp must change an odd number of times. A push at the lamp in row $i$, column $j$ changes exactly the lamps of row $i$ and column $j$.

One push changes only 5 lamps. Two pushes leave a row and a column untouched, so the lamp where they cross stays on. Three pushes in one row (or one column) change every lamp an odd number of times (3 or 1), as needed. So the minimum is 3.

**Answer: (A) 3**

kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-18.title: Start from the squares
kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-18.body:
The neighbours of $n$ are $n - 1$ and $n + 1$. One of them is a square $s$, so $n = s \pm 1$, and the other neighbour is $s \pm 2$, which must be prime. Two-digit $n$ means $s$ is one of 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.

| $s$ | $n = s - 1$, other neighbour $s - 2$ | $n = s + 1$, other neighbour $s + 2$ |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | 8 (not two-digit) | **10**: 11 prime ✓ |
| 16 | 15: 14 ✗ | 17: 18 ✗ |
| 25 | **24**: 23 prime ✓ | 26: 27 ✗ |
| 36 | 35: 34 ✗ | 37: 38 ✗ |
| 49 | **48**: 47 prime ✓ | 50: 51 ✗ |
| 64 | 63: 62 ✗ | 65: 66 ✗ |
| 81 | **80**: 79 prime ✓ | **82**: 83 prime ✓ |
| 100 | 99: 98 ✗ | 101 (not two-digit) |

The numbers are 10, 24, 48, 80 and 82: five of them.

**Answer: (E) 5**

kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-18.title: Parity shortcut
kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-18.body:
The prime neighbour of a two-digit number is at least 9, so it is odd; then $n$ is even and the square neighbour is odd too. So we only need the odd squares 9, 25, 49, 81 and check $s - 2$ and $s + 2$:
- 9: 7 gives $n = 8$ (too small), 11 gives $n = 10$ ✓
- 25: 23 ✓ ($n = 24$), 27 ✗
- 49: 47 ✓ ($n = 48$), 51 ✗
- 81: 79 ✓ ($n = 80$), 83 ✓ ($n = 82$)

Five numbers.

**Answer: (E) 5**

kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-29.title: Count pairs in the wrong order
kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-29.body:
At the start every pair of children is in the wrong order (the taller one stands first), and at the end every pair must be in the right order. Swapping two neighbours changes the order of exactly that one pair and no other. So each of the $\binom{10}{2} = 45$ pairs needs its own swap: at least 45 interchanges.

45 is enough: move the smallest child to the front with 9 swaps, then the next smallest with 8 swaps, and so on: $9 + 8 + \dots + 1 = 45$.

**Answer: (D) 45**

kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-29.title: Small cases
kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-29.body:
With 2 children you need 1 swap, with 3 children 3 swaps ($CBA \to BCA \to BAC \to ABC$), with 4 children 6 swaps. Each new child at the front has to pass all the others: $1 + 2 + \dots + 9 = 45$ for 10 children.

**Answer: (D) 45**

kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-30.title: Angles around E, then around the next vertex
kangaroo-ca-2014-g0708-30.body:
Each angle of a regular pentagon is $\frac{(5-2) \cdot 180°}{5} = 108°$.

**Around $E$.** The two pentagons meet at $E$, the right angle $FEG$ lies between them at the top, and the two congruent triangles fill the rest. So the two triangle angles at $E$ add up to $360° - 108° - 108° - 90° = 54°$, i.e. $27°$ each.

**The triangles.** Let $Q$ be the lower vertex of the left pentagon on its side through $E$, and $P$ the bottom point where the triangles meet. In the picture, triangle $EQP$ has the two shorter sides $EQ$ (a pentagon side) and $QP$ (a trapezoid leg) equal, so its angles at $E$ and $P$ are equal: $27°$ each, and $\angle EQP = 180° - 2 \cdot 27° = 126°$.

**Around $Q$.** The pentagon angle, the triangle angle and the trapezoid angle at $Q$ make a full turn: the trapezoid angle at $Q$ is $360° - 108° - 126° = 126°$. In an isosceles trapezoid the angles along a leg add up to $180°$, so the acute angles are $180° - 126° = 54°$.

**Answer: (C) 54°**
